h1: Parking and access planning for a brewpub site
title: Parking and Access for a Brewpub Site | Craft Beer School
desc: How to judge parking, guest access and delivery routes at a brewpub site, from malt trucks and keg vans to cabs at closing time.
teaser: Guests can find a way in. A 25 kg malt sack, a CO2 cylinder and a water tanker need a plan.
standfirst: A brewpub site is chosen for footfall and rent. It also has to receive grain, kegs, gas and sometimes tankers. Then it has to send guests home safely. Here is what to check before you sign.
sections: Two kinds of traffic, one front door

A restaurant thinks about guests. A brewpub has to think about guests and a small factory's supply chain at the same address. Malt arrives in 25 kg sacks or larger bags, often a few hundred kilos at a time. Hops come chilled. CO2 cylinders come and go. Spent grain leaves, sometimes daily on a busy brewing week. In summer a water tanker may arrive as well.

If every one of those deliveries has to come through the dining room, service suffers and so does hygiene. The ideal site has a separate service entrance close to the brewhouse and the cold room, usable at hours when guests are not there.
Walk the delivery route with a sack on your shoulder

Before signing, physically trace the route from where a delivery vehicle can stop to where the malt store will be. Count the steps, the turns, the doors and their widths. A goods lift or a ramp changes everything. A narrow spiral stair means every grain bill is carried by hand, one sack at a time.

Do the same for the brewhouse vessels themselves. Tanks have to get in once. Fermenters may need to come out again if you ever upgrade. Measure door openings, lift sizes and ceiling heights against the vessel drawings. A fermenter that does not fit through the door is an expensive conversation with a fabricator.
Spent grain is a daily logistics job

A brew of 1,000 litres typically produces somewhere around 200 to 250 kg of wet spent grain. It is heavy, warm and starts to sour within a day in Indian heat. Most brewpubs give it to a local farmer or dairy for cattle feed. That works only if the farmer's vehicle can reach your back door on brew days without blocking traffic or the guest entrance.

Agree the collection time and place before you open. Plan a clean, drained area where bins can wait for a few hours. A pile of souring grain next to a dining terrace will undo a lot of good design.
Guest parking and the honest question

Municipal building rules usually set parking requirements for commercial premises. These vary by city. Your architect will check the site against them. Beyond the legal minimum, ask how your guests will actually arrive. In a city centre, most may come by cab or metro. On a highway or in a suburb, many will drive.

A brewpub has a responsibility here that a café does not. Guests who drive in may want to drive home after drinking. Make it easy not to. Have a cab pick-up point that is visible and well lit. Train staff to offer to book a ride. Some venues partner with driver services that take the guest and their car home. Never encourage anyone to drive after drinking.
Valet, shared parking and the neighbours

Where on-site parking is short, valet parking or an arrangement with a nearby lot can help. Check who is liable for vehicles and keys. Then check what the lease or society rules allow. Cars double-parked outside a residential lane at 11 pm are a common cause of complaints. Our guide on handling noise complaints covers how small frictions like this grow.
Gas, kegs and the cold chain at the door

CO2 cylinders are heavy and must be moved upright on a trolley, never rolled or dropped. A full 30 kg cylinder plus its steel body weighs far more than a sack of malt. Plan a short, level route from the vehicle to a ventilated gas store, chained to the wall. If you buy kegs from other breweries or send your own out, the same route carries 50 litre kegs weighing over 60 kg when full.

Cold chain matters at the door too. Hops and yeast arrive chilled and should go straight into the cold room, not sit on a loading bay in the afternoon sun. A delivery window early in the morning, before the heat and before guests, protects both the ingredients and the dining room.

Step-free access to the entrance, the dining area and at least one accessible toilet should be part of the brief. It widens your customer base and it is increasingly expected in new commercial premises. A ramp is far cheaper at fit out than as a retrofit. Fire exits must also stay clear at all times, which matters when a service entrance doubles as an escape route.
Put access on the drawings and the opening plan

Ask the architect to draw guest flow, delivery flow and waste flow on the site plan in three colours. Where the lines cross, there will be friction. Fix it on paper. Then write delivery windows into supplier agreements before opening, as part of your opening month plan.

Access is one of the questions that separates a pretty site from a workable one. The Brewery Business Management course works through site selection with the costing beside it. Your first step this week: stand at the site at 7 am and at 11 pm and watch who can park, stop and unload.
faqs: Does a brewpub need a separate service entrance?
It is strongly preferred. Malt, kegs, gas and spent grain moving through the dining room hurts both service and hygiene.
How much spent grain does a brewpub produce?
Roughly 200 to 250 kg of wet spent grain for every 1,000 litre brew. It sours quickly in heat, so plan daily collection.
How can a brewpub discourage drink driving?
Offer to book cabs, keep a visible pick-up point and consider partnering with driver services. Never encourage anyone to drive after drinking.
